vignette:
She is sixty-six now, a widowed woman from Oceania who has spent most of her adult life solving problems that move invisibly through cables, routers, and server rooms. As a network engineer, she trusts systems that can be mapped, traced, and repaired. What happened to her does not fit that logic. It remains, in her words, "a breach with no way to isolate the damage."

The assault happens three years after her husband dies. She is already living with the quiet adjustments of widowhood-eating dinner standing at the kitchen counter, falling asleep with the television on, learning how to carry groceries and grief at the same time. One evening she leaves work later than usual after staying to help with a network outage at a regional office. The building is mostly empty. In the parking structure, a man approaches her from behind, asks a question she does not fully hear, then grabs her before she can turn. She remembers the smell of concrete dust, the pressure on her jaw, the shock more than the pain at first. She remembers thinking, with eerie clarity, that no one will know where she is because she had not told anyone she was staying late.

Afterward, she drives home in a state she describes as mechanical, as if her body has taken over while the rest of her has gone offline. She sits in her car in the driveway for nearly an hour, staring at the dashboard clock. In the days that follow, she tells the police, then repeats the story to hospital staff, then to a supervisor. Each telling leaves her feeling less real. People are kind, but she begins to dread their faces tightening with concern. She stops correcting details when they get them wrong. It seems easier to let others hold a blurred version of what happened.

At first she expects the fear to settle. Instead, her world narrows. She stops parking in garages and starts arriving at work before sunrise so she can get a spot near the entrance. If she cannot find one, she drives around the block until she is shaking and late. In meetings, she chooses the chair closest to the door and keeps her laptop bag on her lap like a shield. When male colleagues walk behind her unexpectedly, her whole body jerks. She laughs it off, embarrassed by how visible it is, but the laugh is thin and brittle.

Sleep becomes a nightly negotiation. She checks the locks, then checks them again. She props a chair under the door handle even though she knows, rationally, that it is unnecessary. When she finally lies down, she does not drift so much as brace. Some nights she wakes with her heart pounding, convinced someone is in the room. Other nights she dreams she is back in the parking garage, except in the dream her legs will not move and her dead husband is on the other side of a glass wall, unable to reach her. In the morning she is exhausted and angry at herself for still being affected. She has spent a career staying calm during outages and cyberattacks; she cannot understand why her own nervous system behaves like an unstable network under constant threat.

Her work, once a source of pride, becomes another place where the assault keeps happening in fragments. A dropped metal cart in the server room makes her duck and gasp before she can stop herself. She loses track of commands she has typed thousands of times. She rereads emails without absorbing them. During remote maintenance windows, she used to enjoy the solitude and precision of troubleshooting. Now the silence of empty buildings is unbearable. She volunteers for daytime tasks and invents technical reasons to avoid after-hours site visits. She notices younger coworkers exchanging glances when she forgets things, and shame burns hot in her chest.

Outside work, her life grows smaller. Friends invite her to dinner, but she often declines because she cannot stand the vulnerability of walking alone from a restaurant to her car. She used to attend community gatherings and ocean festivals that reminded her of home; now crowds feel dangerous and open spaces feel exposed. Her daughter, who lives in another city, tells her she sounds far away on the phone. She says she is just tired. It is easier than explaining that she no longer feels at home in her own body.

What troubles her most is not only fear but the way the assault has altered her sense of self. She was once decisive, dryly funny, dependable in a crisis. Now she startles at footsteps, scans every room for exits, and mistrusts moments that should be ordinary. If a stranger stands too close in a queue, her skin prickles. If she sees a man in a dark jacket near her apartment entrance, she circles the block rather than risk passing him. She tells herself she is being sensible, but part of her grieves how much of her life is organized around avoiding reminders she cannot fully predict.

In quieter moments, she speaks of loneliness in a way that seems deeper than being widowed or living alone. Since the assault, she feels separated from other people by something invisible but absolute. She can describe the event clearly enough, yet what stays with her is harder to put into words: the constant anticipation, the collapse of trust, the humiliating certainty that danger can erupt into any ordinary evening and leave the whole structure of a life permanently changed.
